Filtering with a Conditional where →

Scoping a Nested Lookup

Two things a nested URL has to check that a flat one doesn't: does the parent exist, and does the child actually belong to it.

A flat resource like Tag only ever has one thing to check before an update or delete: does this id exist (previous "Read Before Write" slide). A nested resource like Comment has a second question sitting right next to it — /tickets/1/comments/9 names two ids, and both have to be right, not just individually valid. comment.controller.js checks the parent first, using the exact same ticketService.getTicketById every ticket route already calls:

// Figure 3.12: confirming the parent exists, then scoping the child lookup (src/controllers/comment.controller.js and src/services/comment.service.js, excerpt)
const findTicketOr404 = async (ticketId) => {
  const ticket = await ticketService.getTicketById(ticketId);
  if (!ticket) throw new ApiError(404, `Ticket ${ticketId} not found`);
};

export const getCommentById = async (ticketId, id) =>
  prisma.comment.findFirst({
    where: { id, ticketId },
    include: { author: authorSummary },
  });

findTicketOr404 runs at the top of every comment controller function — list, get, create, update, delete — so a request under a ticket that doesn't exist (or was deleted) 404s on the ticket, before ever touching Comment at all.

The second check is subtler: Comment.id is already a unique primary key on its own, so prisma.comment.findUnique({ where: { id } }) would find comment 9 regardless of which ticket it actually belongs to — a request for /tickets/1/comments/9 would happily return a comment that's really attached to ticket 47. findFirst({ where: { id, ticketId } }) closes that gap by scoping the lookup to both — if comment 9 belongs to ticket 47, a request naming ticket 1 finds nothing and reaches the controller's own 404, exactly as if the comment didn't exist. getCommentsByTicketId (this lesson's list endpoint) never had this problem in the first place — it only ever queries where: { ticketId } to begin with — but any lookup of one specific nested item needs this extra scoping to stay correct.
